title: DPDP Rules: Consent Manager Registration Framework Takes Effect From 13 November 2026
meta_description: The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules provisions on registering and operating Consent Managers come into force on 13 November 2026.
court: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (regulatory development, not a court ruling)
case_name: Not applicable; Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 4 commencement
citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, notified 13 November 2025 under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; Rule 4 (Consent Managers) effective 13 November 2026
body: A second compliance milestone under India's data protection law arrives this week. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 on 13 November 2025, bringing some provisions into force immediately while staggering others over the following eighteen months. Rule 4, which sets out the framework for registering and operating Consent Managers, is the next provision scheduled to commence, one year after notification, on 13 November 2026.

Under the DPDP Act and Rules, a Consent Manager is an intermediary a person (called a Data Principal under the Act) can use to give, manage, review and withdraw consent for the processing of personal data across different data fiduciaries through a single, interoperable interface. The idea borrows from the consent architecture built for India's financial data-sharing systems, extended here to personal data processing generally. Instead of a person tracking separate consent settings on every app, website or service that collects their data, a registered Consent Manager is meant to give them one place to see what they have agreed to and to withdraw that agreement.

Until now, that framework existed only on paper, since no provision had come into force letting an entity actually register as a Consent Manager or operate under the Board's supervision. The commencement of Rule 4 changes that, moving the Consent Manager concept from a defined but dormant piece of the Act into something an entity can apply for and the Data Protection Board can approve, reject or revoke.

From 13 November 2026, an entity wanting to operate as a Consent Manager must register with the Data Protection Board of India under the conditions Rule 4 and its accompanying schedule set out. Reported requirements include incorporation as an Indian company, a minimum net worth threshold, and technical and operational standards for how the Consent Manager's platform must interoperate with data fiduciaries and represent a person's consent choices clearly and in one place.

The provision sits within a staggered commencement structure that the MeitY notification set out from the start. Some obligations, including the constitution of the Data Protection Board itself, took effect alongside the November 2025 notification. The remaining core compliance obligations on data fiduciaries, covering notice requirements, verifiable consent, data breach reporting and reasonable security safeguards under Rule 3, are scheduled to commence roughly eighteen months after notification, in May 2027.

For businesses that process personal data, the Consent Manager framework commencing this week does not itself impose a new direct compliance obligation on an ordinary data fiduciary, since registering and operating as a Consent Manager is a separate, licensed role rather than something every business must do. What changes from 13 November 2026 is that the regulatory pathway for Consent Manager applicants becomes operative, and any business planning to integrate with or rely on a registered Consent Manager for consent collection should track whether its chosen provider has actually registered under the new framework rather than merely announced an intention to do so.

Businesses in Delhi NCR and Kolkata operating consumer apps, fintech platforms, healthcare portals or e-commerce services that currently manage consent through in-house mechanisms should treat this commencement date as a point to review their consent architecture against where the law is heading, even though the broader notice-and-consent obligations under Rule 3 are still roughly six months away. Waiting until May 2027 to begin that review leaves little room to test integrations or vendor contracts before the fuller compliance regime takes hold.

Reports on the exact commencement date differ by a day, with some sources citing 13 November and others 14 November 2026, tracing back to a similar one-day discrepancy in how the original 2025 notification date is recorded across the Gazette publication and the Press Information Bureau release. A business relying on the precise date for a registration deadline should confirm it against the Gazette notification itself rather than secondary commentary, since a one-day error could matter if an internal compliance deadline is pegged directly to the commencement date rather than to the broader milestone itself.
why_it_matters: This is the second of three staggered DPDP compliance milestones, and it specifically opens the door for Consent Managers to register and begin operating under the Data Protection Board's oversight. Businesses that outsource or plan to outsource consent collection to a third-party Consent Manager should confirm that provider's registration status from this date, and all data fiduciaries should use the milestone as a checkpoint before the fuller Rule 3 obligations on notice, consent and breach reporting arrive in May 2027.
card_summary: DPDP Rules provisions on registering and operating Consent Managers take effect from 13 November 2026, opening the pathway for third-party consent intermediaries under Data Protection Board oversight.
card_tip: Before relying on a third-party Consent Manager for consent collection, confirm it is actually registered with the Data Protection Board under Rule 4, not just announced as a provider.
verification_notes: Chosen because the DPDP Act's phased rollout is the single most consequential data protection development for Indian businesses this year, and the Consent Manager commencement date falls within this run's window (13 November 2026, two days after this run). The site has a long-form article on the DPDP compliance clock generally but no News or Updates item specifically marking this commencement date, and no blog guide on Consent Manager obligations, so this is not a duplicate. The 13 November 2026 effective date for Rule 4 and the one-year-after-notification structure are confirmed across three independent law-firm sources (SSRANA, AMSShardul, Lexplosion). A one-day discrepancy (13 versus 14 November) traced to differing readings of the original 2025 notification date across sources is disclosed in the body rather than resolved, since no primary Gazette text was independently checked in this run. No Delhi NCR or Kolkata specific angle exists for a national regulatory commencement; none is forced, though the body notes the businesses most affected in those markets.
